cavaliers flock together, and as they do not like fetching a walk with the absurd woman-
kind, Jane (i.e. Mrs. Williams) and I are off together, and talk morality and pluck violets
by the way’ (Mary to Marianne Hunt, 4 March 1822, Mary L i 221). A period followed of
constant dining together, with lunches and regular long extravagant dinners at the Palazzo
Lanfranchi, walks and horse-riding, soirées and festivities with various members of culti-
vated Pisan society and its small English community, and frequent expeditions to practice
pistol-shooting just outside the city with Byron and his entourage. The men and women
very often went together to the opera in the evenings (see C. L. Cline, Byron, Shelley, and
their Pisan Circle, 1952).
